title: Tragedy as a genre
keyIdea: In the tradition that runs from Aristotle's Poetics through Shakespeare to Arthur Miller, tragedy is not just a sad story. It shows a hero of some greatness whose own error or flaw (hamartia) sets off a fall: fortune reverses (peripeteia), the hero comes to see the truth (anagnorisis), the play ends in catastrophe, and the audience is moved to pity and fear, which Aristotle said are released or clarified (catharsis). Writers have reshaped every part of this pattern, so the definition is a lens to argue with, not a checklist.

kid: A sad story and a tragedy are not the same. If a hiker is hit by lightning, that is sad, but nothing he chose made it happen. In a tragedy, the hero's own choice starts the fall. Macbeth chooses to kill the king, and that choice ruins him.

Aristotle gave us the key words. Hamartia is the hero's error or flaw: Macbeth's ambition, Othello's jealousy, Lear's pride. It is not the same as being evil. The hero is mostly good, and often great, which is why the fall hurts to watch.

The plot turns twice. Peripeteia is the reversal, when fortune swings the other way. Anagnorisis is recognition, when the hero finally sees the truth, often too late. Then comes the catastrophe, the final ruin.

Catharsis happens in us, not on stage. Aristotle said tragedy should make us feel pity, because the hero suffers more than he deserves, and fear, because he is like us. Later writers changed the rules: Arthur Miller made a salesman his tragic hero.
adult: Tragedy is a named genre study in A-level English Literature (for example AQA's Aspects of tragedy). Students must use the terms from Aristotle's Poetics. They apply them to set texts such as Othello, King Lear or Death of a Salesman. Then they judge how far each play fits, bends or breaks the pattern.

The terms are precise. Hamartia means an error or failing, not just a vice. Peripeteia is a reversal of fortune. Anagnorisis is a change from not knowing to knowing. Aristotle thought the best plots join the two, as in Oedipus. Catharsis is still argued over: it may mean a purging, a cleansing or a clearing of pity and fear.

Common mistakes: calling any death or sad ending tragic; treating hamartia as the villain or as bad luck; putting catharsis in the plot, not in the audience; and using the old rules as a checklist. Strong essays test the model. Miller's essay Tragedy and the Common Man rejects the rule that heroes must be high born. Iago's plotting makes Othello's share of the blame a real question.

In the lab students swipe events into sad or tragic. They drag a fortune line into the tragic arc and test it, pin the right flaw on three of Shakespeare's heroes, and name the turning points in Othello. Last, they change a hero's traits until Aristotle's pity and fear meters both fill.

familyTip: Watch or read any tragedy together (a film counts) and ask three questions at the end: what choice of the hero's started the fall, when did everything turn, and when did the hero finally understand? If the answers are 'nothing, never, never', you may have a sad story rather than a tragedy, which is a good argument to have.

visual.caption: Which part of the tragic pattern is it? Drag each moment, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Lear's need to hear his daughters flatter him
Othello swallows Iago's lie and turns on Desdemona
The messenger's good news ruins Oedipus instead
Oedipus learns the man he killed was his father
Lear sees, too late, that Cordelia loved him truly

lab.caption: Flagship lab: judge sad or tragic, shape the tragic arc, pin each hero's hamartia, name Othello's turns and tune pity and fear.

practice.prompt: A character is killed in a random accident in the final scene. Why is this not tragic in Aristotle's sense?
choices: No error or choice of the character's causes the fall
Accidents are too exciting for tragedy
Tragedies cannot end with a death
practice.hint: Ask what drives the fall: chance, or the hero's own hamartia?
practice.explain: Chance suffering is pathetic, not tragic. In Aristotle's model the fall grows out of the hero's own error, so we see cause and effect.

practice.prompt: An essay says, "{n} characters die by the end of Hamlet, so it is a tragedy." What is the weakness?
choices: A body count is not a definition; it should show hamartia, reversal and recognition
It should count the deaths more carefully
Hamlet is a comedy, so the claim is wrong
practice.hint: Would a war film with {n} deaths automatically be a tragedy?
practice.explain: Deaths alone prove nothing. Argue from Hamlet's delay as a possible hamartia, the reversal after the play scene, and his late recognition.

practice.prompt: Neoclassical critics read the Poetics as limiting a tragedy's action to one day (24 hours), the unity of time. A play's action spans {d} days. By how many hours does it break that limit?
practice.hint: Work out the total hours in {d} days, then take away the 24 allowed.
practice.explain: {d} days is {=24*d} hours, so it is {=24*d-24} hours over. Shakespeare ignores the unity: The Winter's Tale leaps sixteen years.

practice.prompt: Oedipus discovers that the man he killed was his own father. Which term fits this moment?
choices: Anagnorisis
Catharsis
Hamartia
practice.hint: Which term means a change from ignorance to knowledge?
practice.explain: Anagnorisis is recognition. In Oedipus it arrives together with the reversal, which Aristotle thought the finest kind of plot.

choices: An error or flaw in the hero that leads to the fall
The villain who destroys the hero
The audience's release of emotion
pool.hint: It belongs to the hero, not to another character or the audience.
pool.explain: Hamartia is the hero's own error or failing, such as Macbeth's ambition. A villain may exploit it, as Iago does, but it is not the villain.

choices: In the audience, as pity and fear are released or clarified
On stage, in the final death scene
In the hero's mind, at the moment of recognition
pool.hint: Aristotle describes what tragedy does to the people watching it.
pool.explain: Catharsis is the audience's response. Placing it in the plot confuses it with catastrophe or anagnorisis.

pool.prompt: Why does Aristotle reject a thoroughly wicked hero?
choices: His fall feels deserved, so it stirs neither pity nor fear
Wicked characters cannot speak in verse
Audiences refuse to watch villains
pool.hint: Pity is for suffering that is more than the person deserves.
pool.explain: We feel pity for undeserved suffering and fear for someone like us. A villain's punishment gives satisfaction instead.

pool.prompt: Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman makes Willy Loman, an ordinary salesman, its tragic hero. Which classical idea does it challenge?
choices: That a tragic hero must be of high status
That a tragedy needs a reversal
That plays are written in acts
pool.hint: Compare Willy with Oedipus, Lear and Macbeth. What do those three have that he lacks?
pool.explain: In 'Tragedy and the Common Man' Miller argues the common man is as apt a subject for tragedy as kings, rejecting the high-status rule.

pool.prompt: In Othello, which moment is best read as the peripeteia?
choices: Act 3, when Othello accepts Iago's lies and vows revenge
Act 1, when Othello and Desdemona marry
After the play, when the audience leaves
pool.hint: Peripeteia is the reversal, when fortune starts to swing the other way.
pool.explain: In the temptation scene of Act 3, Othello's fortune turns from love and success towards murder and ruin. That is the reversal.

pool.prompt: A student argues that Othello has no hamartia because Iago causes everything. What is the strongest reply?
choices: Iago exploits Othello's jealousy and credulity, but Othello still chooses to kill
Othello is the villain of the play
Iago is the real tragic hero
pool.hint: Can a villain's plot and a hero's flaw both be true at once?
pool.explain: Tragedy can share responsibility. Iago lights the fuse, but Othello's readiness to believe and his choice to act make the fall his own.

pool.prompt: A film shows a family losing their home in an earthquake after {n} minutes. Using Aristotle's terms, how is it best described?
choices: Pathos: suffering from chance, with no hamartia
Tragedy, because the ending is unhappy
Catharsis, because it is upsetting
pool.hint: Did anyone's error cause the earthquake?
pool.explain: It may be deeply moving, but the suffering comes from chance, not from a hero's error, so it is pathos rather than tragedy.

pool.prompt: A {n}-word essay calls Lear's banishing of Cordelia in Act 1 his anagnorisis. What is the slip?
choices: Banishing her is the hamartia in action; the recognition comes later, when he sees she loved him
There is no slip: banishing her is the recognition
Lear has no recognition in the play
pool.hint: Recognition means coming to see the truth. Does Lear see clearly when he banishes her?
pool.explain: In Act 1 Lear's pride blinds him. His recognition comes in Act 4, waking to Cordelia, too late to save either of them.
